chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from Zurara, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), 'Is the borrowed item (for use) under guarantee?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'For all that you borrow, if it is damaged, you are not liable for its damage except for gold and silver, for these two are liable (for damage) unless it is stipulated that whenever they are damaged, their damage is not liable upon you; and similarly, for all that you borrow, if it is stipulated upon you, it is liable upon you; and gold and silver are liable upon you even if it is not stipulated upon you.'
ai.seo_question: What is the borrower's liability for damage to a borrowed item in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi delineates the principle of 'daman' (guarantee) in 'al-'ariyyah' (gratuitous loan), establishing that gold and silver are inherently liable for loss due to their fungible nature, whereas other items are only liable if specifically stipulated. This ruling reflects the Shia juristic distinction between items where value is intrinsic versus those where value is derived from utility, a nuance critical in Usuli fiqh. The text underscores the flexibility of contractual stipulations (shurut) in modifying default legal presumptions, highlighting the importance of mutual agreement in civil transactions.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Jameel, from Zurara who said,

‘I said to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, ‘The borrowed item is under guarantee?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The entirety of what is borrowed, and it gets damaged, so you are not necessitated for its damage except for the gold and the silver, for these two both necessitate (a guarantee), except if there is a stipulation upon it that when these two are damaged so its damage would not be necessitated upon you; and similar to that is the entirety of what is borrowed, and it is stipulated upon you for obligating you; and the gold and the silver (its guarantee) is obligated for you and even if there is no such stipulation upon you’.
en.sarwar: 3. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from Jamil from Zurarah who has said the following: “This is concerning my question before abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the borrowed item; if the borrower was held liable for it.

He (the Imam) said, ‘If whatever you borrow is destroyed, you are not held liable except gold and silver; which bring liability unless it is stipulated that even on being destroyed you are not held liable. You are held liable for all that you borrow and it is stipulated that you are liable. Gold and silver bring liability, even if no stipulation is set.’”
